SM20A-B1.free_elimination: 64/9 and 256/9 struck by the stem premise: the stem asks 'How many bacteria', a count, so the two non-integer options die at a glance. Remaining 16 vs 24 is the real decision (24 = P(1), dividing by b once). All options < 36, so the growth bound kills nothing.
SM20A-B1.note: Cold: b^2 = 81/36 = 9/4, b = 3/2, a = 36/(9/4) = 16. Key correct and unique; all distractor_solve values reproduce. Two strikes come from one cause (count phrasing + fractional distractors), so no single-distractor swap fixes both. Preferred repair: change the question to 'What is the value of a?' (removes the integrality premise; a continuous constant may be fractional) - then no class strikes any option. If the stem must stay, replace 256/9 with 4 (drops the denominator of 9/4, takes b^2 = 9, a = 36/9 = 4): integer, positive, < 36, not a sum/difference/mean/product of others in {4, 16, 24, 64/9}; 64/9 would still die by integrality (n_struck 1).

SM20A-B2.free_elimination: none. Checked closure ({-14/3,-3,10/3,11/3}: no sum/difference/mean/double of two others equals a third), sign (sum of roots unconstrained), printed numbers (11/3 needs moving the x term, not read off the stem). 10/3/11/3 differ by 1/3 but that does not identify which is the key.
SM20A-B2.note: Cold: 3x^2 - 10x - 8 = x + 6 -> 3x^2 - 11x - 14 = 0 = (3x - 14)(x + 1); roots 14/3, -1; sum 11/3. All distractors reproduce (10/3 = sum of LHS roots / x term not moved, -3 sign error, -14/3 product). Borderline easy: with Desmos, graphing both sides shows intersections at -1 and 4.667 directly, so 'medium' only for a hand solver. No repair needed.

SM20A-B3.free_elimination: 5/3 struck by integrality: 3 visibly divides 6 and 5 visibly divides -20, so a and m are integers and k = am + 15 is an integer; the lone fraction dies at a glance. (In practice a = 2, m = -4 are themselves glances, so the whole item is near-glance.)
SM20A-B3.note: Cold: 3a = 6 -> a = 2; 5m = -20 -> m = -4; k = am + 15 = 7. All distractors reproduce. Honest difficulty is easy (two one-step divisions and one product), not medium. Repair for the strike: replace 5/3 with 23 (sign slip on the cross term, k = 15 - am = 15 + 8): integer, so the integrality class no longer fires; in {-2, 3, 7, 23} 23 is not a sum/difference/mean/double/product of two others (3*7 = 21, 3+7 = 10, 7-(-2) = 9). To reach medium, make a not visibly integral, e.g. (ax + 5)(3x + m) with leading 6x^2 and constant -20 replaced so that a and m require the cross term to determine (e.g. give k and ask for a).

SM20A-B4.free_elimination: none at a glance. -21/4 is not killed by sign (the graph is >= 0 but a slope-1 line with negative intercept still meets it); 4 is not killed without checking y = x + 4 against the arch over all x; 1 is a genuine valid value (three points: x = -1, 2, 4) but not the greatest, so it is the intended lure, not a second answer under 'greatest'.
SM20A-B4.note: Cold: arch y = -x^2 + 2x + 3 on (-1,3), peak (1,4). Tangent to arch: x^2 - x + (b - 3) = 0, disc 0 -> b = 13/4, tangency x = 1/2 inside the arch; outer branches give x = (3 +/- sqrt34)/2, both outside [-1,3] -> 3 points. b = 1 (through (-1,0)) also gives 3 points (x = -1, 2, 4); b = -3 gives 1; b = 4 gives 2. Greatest = 13/4. Distractors all reproduce. Algebraically this is a real hard item (reflection + tangency + corner case), but under the brief's Desmos assumption a student graphs y = |x^2-2x-3| and each of the four lines and counts intersections (4 -> 2, 13/4 -> 3, 1 -> 3, -21/4 -> 1), then takes the greatest: option plug-back bypasses the decision. Reported medium for that reason; it is the hardest item in this half. No option repair needed; to resist Desmos plug-back, ask for 'the sum of all values of b' (= 1 + 13/4 = 17/4) so the student must find both cases, with distractors 13/4, 1, and -21/4+13/4 = -2.

SM20A-B5.free_elimination: 2 struck by the vertex bound: axis t = 88/32 = 2.75, and 'on its way down' must be after it. Then a mirror-pair tell: 2 and 3.5 are symmetric about 2.75, so they are visibly the two roots of h(t) = c for one height; with 2 on the way up, its mirror 3.5 is the way-down time, killing 6.5 and 8 without solving (6.5's mirror is -1, 8's is -2.5, neither present). Robust strike count 1 (the axis bound); the pair tell takes it to 3.
SM20A-B5.note: Cold: -16t^2 + 88t - 112 = 0 -> 2t^2 - 11t + 14 = 0 -> (2t - 7)(t - 2) -> t = 2, 3.5; later = 3.5. Landing 2t^2 - 11t - 13 = 0 -> 6.5; distractor 8 reproduces from +216. Max height 225 > 216, premise consistent. Repair (one distractor): replace 2 with 5.5, the time the ball returns to roof height (set h = 104, -16t^2 + 88t = 0, t = 88/16), a reachable 'wrong target height' slip. Then every option is after the vertex (axis bound kills nothing), no two options are symmetric about 2.75 (mirror of 5.5 is 0), and in {3.5, 5.5, 6.5, 8} no option is a sum/difference/mean/double of two others (mean(3.5,8) = 5.75, mean(5.5,6.5) = 6, 8-6.5 = 1.5). Cost: loses the rising-root lure; 5.5 replaces it as a target-height error.

SM20A-B6.free_elimination: 5 struck by glance plug-back: the second equation with x = 5 forces 9^y = 1, y = 0, and then the first reads 2^5 = 16^5, visibly false. 5 is also a printed exponent. 33/5 and 35/4 need the base conversion to test, so they survive.
SM20A-B6.note: Cold: x + 3y = 20, x - 2y = 5 -> y = 3, x = 11. Check 2^11 * 8^3 = 2^20. All distractors reproduce. Repair: replace 5 with 13, from writing 8^y as 2^(y+3) (x + y + 3 = 20, with x - 2y = 5 -> y = 4, x = 13). Plug-back of 13 needs y = 4 and 2^13 * 2^12 = 2^25 vs 2^20, i.e. the full base conversion, so not a glance; 13 is not printed; in {11, 13, 33/5, 35/4} no option is a sum/difference/mean/double of two others (mean(11,13) = 12, 13-11 = 2). Note the key would then not be the largest option, which also removes a mild 'largest integer' look.

SM20A-B7.free_elimination: 240 struck by monotonicity: Q multiplies by 1.3, less than P's 1.69 per 120 months, so Q's period must be shorter than 120 months; any k >= 120 dies at a glance. 1200/23 (~52) and 1200/13 (~92) survive the bound; they look contrived (decimal bases appearing in denominators) but no class kills them logically.
SM20A-B7.note: Cold: 1.69 = 1.3^2, so P = 4000(1.3)^(t/5), period 5 years = 60 months, k = 60. Distractors reproduce, but 1200/23 and 1200/13 encode implausible mistakes (scaling the period by 30/69 or 1.3/1.69) that real students rarely make, and the two natural traps are absent: forgetting the square (k = 120) and forgetting months (k = 5). Because no option catches the obvious slip, a student who errs re-checks rather than lands on a distractor -> not hard by the brief's definition; Desmos (solve 1.69 = 1.3^(120/k)) also bypasses. Repair (one distractor): replace 240 with 5 (period in years, no month conversion). 5 < 120 survives monotonicity; not printed; not a sum/mean/difference/double of two others. Caveat: 60 = 12 * 5 makes key-is-12x-a-distractor visible, a weak tell; 120 cannot be used as it dies to the same monotonicity bound.
